body:
# Best Budget Hammock Underquilts — Fixing Cold Butt Syndrome

You picked a hammock, hung it well, climbed in with your sleeping bag, and woke at 3 a.m. with a cold strip running from shoulders to heels. That is cold butt syndrome, and nearly every new hammock camper runs into it. Your sleeping bag isn't defective. The problem is physics.

A sleeping bag keeps you warm by trapping air in its loft. When you lie in a hammock, your body weight flattens the insulation underneath you to almost nothing. Compressed insulation traps very little air, so the hammock fabric and the moving air below pull heat straight out of your back. An underquilt fixes this by hanging *outside* the hammock, snug against its underside, where nothing crushes it. The loft stays full, and your back gets the insulation the sleeping bag can no longer provide.

If you haven't bought the hammock yet, start with our guide to [the best cheap camping hammocks](/blog/best-camping-hammocks-under-50). This guide picks up from there.

## Underquilt vs Pad: Which Should You Use?

A sleeping pad inside the hammock is the cheaper route, and it does work. A pad doesn't rely on loft the way a bag does, so it still insulates when you lie on it. The drawbacks are specific to hammocks:

- **Pads slide.** On a curved, swaying surface a pad migrates out from under you overnight, often leaving your hips or shoulders exposed.
- **Pads fight the hammock's shape.** A flat, stiff pad keeps you from settling into the diagonal lay that makes a hammock comfortable.
- **Shoulders hang off.** Most pads are narrower than your body in a hammock, so your shoulders touch bare fabric.

An underquilt wraps the whole underside, doesn't move when you do, and leaves the inside of the hammock free. Many budget hammock campers use a pad first and add an underquilt once the nights get colder. That's a sensible order. You can also combine the two on cold nights. If you go the pad route, our [budget sleeping pad guide](/blog/best-budget-sleeping-pads-under-50) covers the options.

**One firm warning:** a mylar emergency blanket or "space blanket" is not insulation. It has no loft. Laying one in or under your hammock won't replace an underquilt or a pad, and you shouldn't count on it to keep you warm overnight.

## How to Choose a Budget Underquilt

**Read temperature ratings carefully.** Sleeping gear ratings usually come in two kinds. A *comfort* rating is the temperature where a typical sleeper stays comfortable. A *limit* rating is closer to the point where you get through the night cold and miserable. Budget listings often give one number without saying which kind it is. Assume it's the optimistic one. Plan for nights noticeably warmer than whatever number is printed. No underquilt adds a guaranteed number of degrees to your setup. Warmth depends on how well the quilt fits, the wind, the humidity, what you're wearing, and your own metabolism.

**Check fit and length.** A full-length underquilt covers you from head to foot. Some budget quilts run shorter and leave your feet to the sleeping bag alone. Confirm the quilt suits your hammock's size. The listing should say whether it fits single hammocks, double hammocks, or both.

**Look at the suspension.** Underquilts hang from cords at each end and usually use shock cord or drawstrings to pull them up against the hammock. Gaps between the quilt and the hammock let cold air in, so adjustability matters more than almost any other feature.

**Mind the weather above you.** An underquilt can't do its job if wind is stripping heat away or rain is soaking it. A tarp overhead does a lot of the work. That's why one appears in the picks below.

**Dress in the right layers.** Wear synthetic or wool base layers to bed. Never use cotton as a warmth layer. It holds moisture against your skin and pulls heat away.

## The Picks

### Gold Armour Hammock Underquilt

The Gold Armour underquilt is listed as fitting both single and double hammocks, which makes it a flexible first underquilt if you haven't settled on a hammock size or plan to upgrade later. The listing describes it as insulated and presents it as an essential piece of hammock camping gear. It comes in a grey and sky blue colorway.

It's a strong match for the shoulder-season camper who keeps waking up cold in a hammock that's otherwise comfortable. The listing doesn't state a temperature rating, so don't assume one. Start with mild nights, see how you sleep, and work outward from there.

**[Check the Gold Armour Hammock Underquilt on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07C1XP4RF?tag=camprally-20)**

### Wise Owl Outfitters Hammock Underquilt

Wise Owl Outfitters is a familiar name in budget hammocks. If you already own one of their hammocks, keeping the system in one brand is convenient. The listing calls this underquilt insulated, ultralight, water-resistant, and packable, so it suits backpackers who are counting space and weight.

Water-resistant isn't waterproof. Treat the shell as protection against dew and condensation, not against rain, and pitch a tarp overhead. No temperature figure is given here either, so plan conservatively for your first cold trips.

**[Check the Wise Owl Outfitters Hammock Underquilt on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08GD3MD7B?tag=camprally-20)**

### onewind 12×10ft Ultralight Camping Hammock Tarp

This one isn't an underquilt, and that's the point. Wind blowing across the underside of a hammock is one of the biggest heat thieves there is, and rain soaking an underquilt cancels out its insulation. A tarp handles both.

The onewind tarp is listed at 12×10 feet with doors. Doors are the feature that matters for cold nights: closing the ends cuts the wind that would otherwise funnel along the hammock and across your underquilt. The listing describes it as ultralight. If your budget only stretches to one upgrade and your nights are windy rather than truly cold, a tarp with doors may help more than you'd expect. For pitching techniques, see [how to set up a camping tarp](/blog/how-to-set-up-a-camping-tarp).

**[Check the onewind 12×10ft Ultralight Camping Hammock Tarp on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B087BL2S4Y?tag=camprally-20)**

### DD Hammocks Underblanket

DD Hammocks markets this underblanket for fall and winter camping. It's the only pick here whose listing states a temperature: suitable to 23 degrees Fahrenheit. The listing doesn't say whether that's a comfort or a limit figure, so read it as the edge of what the product can handle, not a comfortable night's sleep. If you're new to hammocks, don't take it anywhere near that temperature until you've learned how your own setup performs on milder nights, and bring a backup such as an insulated pad.

It's described as lightweight and portable. It makes sense for campers who want something clearly aimed at colder seasons rather than a summer-weight quilt.

**[Check the DD Hammocks Underblanket on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00KG9V93C?tag=camprally-20)**

### Camping Hammock, 772 lbs Capacity Double Hammock

If your underquilt choice is pushing you toward a new hammock, this double hammock is listed with a 772-pound capacity. A double-width body gives you room for a proper diagonal lay. Lying flatter makes the hammock more comfortable and helps an underquilt sit evenly across your back instead of bunching at the sides.

Before you buy, confirm that whichever underquilt you choose fits a double hammock. The Gold Armour pick above lists both sizes. The listing calls the color black.

**[Check the Camping Hammock, 772 lbs Capacity Double Hammock on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07P11P7H4?tag=camprally-20)**

### OneTigris Hideout Hammock Underquilt

OneTigris markets the Hideout as lightweight 4-season hammock gear. The listing pitches it for camping, hiking, backpacking, travel, beach, backyard, and patio use. It's a good choice if you want one underquilt that covers casual backyard lounging as well as overnight trips.

Be careful with the "4 season" label. Without a stated temperature rating, it tells you the product is *marketed* for year-round use, not what conditions it will keep you warm in. Winter hammock camping punishes optimistic assumptions. If you're heading into real cold, read [winter camping for beginners](/blog/winter-camping-for-beginners) first and layer this quilt with a pad and a warm sleeping bag.

**[Check the OneTigris Hideout Hammock Underquilt on Amazon](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B08936QVJD?tag=camprally-20)**

## Verdict

- **Most flexible first underquilt:** the **Gold Armour**, because it's listed for both single and double hammocks.
- **Lightest pack:** the **Wise Owl Outfitters** quilt, which is listed as ultralight, packable, and water-resistant.
- **Colder trips:** the **DD Hammocks Underblanket**. It's the only pick with a stated rating (23°F). Treat that number as a limit, not a promise.
- **Year-round casual use:** the **OneTigris Hideout**. Back it up with other layers when it gets cold.

Don't skip the **onewind tarp**. Blocking wind and rain lets any underquilt perform as designed.

Whatever you buy, build your setup in layers: an underquilt or pad beneath you, a tarp above, and a bag plus non-cotton clothing in between. Try it in the backyard or on a mild night before you trust it on a cold one.
